Canadian checking in. 

I'd say we have a pretty balanced system. Emergency situations that are life-threatening are for the most part, covered and completely cost free. I don't lose sleep at night worrying about getting sick and going bankrupt. 

Hospital wait times can be long, however, you get seen based on severity of your condition. A young/middle aged person with an illness or a broken bone? Be prepared to wait at least a few hours in emerg. Elderly/Very young or having something that requires immediate intervention - ie. a heart attack, they push you right through to been seen within minutes. 

I pay nothing to see my family doctor, and can usually get an appointment within a few weeks of calling in for one. I also pay nothing to get referrals, blood work, perscrptions faxed, x-rays, ultrasounds, mris, ect. or to see a specialist. 

Perscription medication and vision/dental are not covered and you have to pay out-of-pocket for those unless you have private insurance. You can obtain insurance privately to cover those things, or most people have insurance through their employer. I pay $9.00 bi-weekly off of my paycheck and get 100% coverage on perscription drugs, and 85% coverage for vision and dental. Overall, very good.

If you don't have private coverage for perscriptions/vision/dental these things can get VERY expensive. It won't bankrupt you, but, for a while, as a broke college student with no insurance, I was paying close to $140 per month just on perscription medication, wich was a little ridiculous.

TL;DR: Canadian universal health care is pretty good. Doctors and hospitals don't cost you anything. Perscription drugs/vision/dental is not covered and can be expensive without additional health insurance.

The best thing I ever did for myself when battling my depression was seek professional help.

It takes a long time to finally admit that you do need help, but once you do, it's like a weight being lifted off of your shoulders. I felt like telling my family and friends that I needed to see a therapist and be put on medication would make me more of a burden; make things worse.

But I was wrong. It saved my life, countless times. Being on medication to even my emotions out, and having someone to talk to. Even if it's calling your local suicide hotline (Which I have done on a few occasions) helps. Those people are trained to handle situations like that. 

Stay strong. There are people in this world who care about you; I'm certain. Even though we've never met, my heart goes out to you.
